You are solving a Magic: The Gathering puzzle.

You have access to local read-only tools, if you want to refer to the full rules:
- grep(path, pattern): search a file and return matching lines with line numbers
- read(path, line_number, num_lines): read a window of lines from a file

The comprehensive rules are available at this absolute path:
comp_rules.txt

Puzzle conventions:
Winning
Unless otherwise stated, you must win the puzzle by inflicting lethal damage to your opponent before the turn ends. This can be as late as during the cleanup step if necessary. Your solution must work for all possible outcomes, such as your opponent’s actions and blocking decisions (see below.)
Phase
Unless otherwise stated, you begin each puzzle at the beginning of your first main phase. You have already drawn a card and gone past upkeep triggers. You have not yet played a land, cast any spells, activated any abilities of permanents on the battlefield, or attacked.
Your Opponent’s Resources / Actions
Unless otherwise stated, your opponent has no cards in hand and no other permanents in play (including no lands – despite the lack of realism there.) This means the only actions you need to consider are activated abilities with no mana cost. Most puzzles with opponent actions will offer more information on this.
Blocking
You cannot assume that your opponent will block a certain way, unless they are somehow forced to. Your solution must satisfy all possible blocking scenarios, even ones that would seem strange in a regular game, and always deal lethal in order to be correct.
Dice
Sometimes you will see six-sided dice placed on cards. These are meant to indicate counters, of whatever type is most reasonable to be there. On most creatures they will be +1/+1 counters, on most artifacts and lands they will be charge counters, and on most Planeswalkers they will be loyalty counters.
If the card specifies a type of counter itself, however (like Icatian Javelineers or Raging Ravine), that will dictate which type it is. 
For -1/-1 counters, we will use a separate graphic to avoid confusion.
Zones
Unless otherwise stated, all zones not displayed are empty. Neither you nor your opponent have cards in graveyards or in exile.
Cards Drawn from Libraries
In any puzzle in which either player might draw cards or otherwise access their library, the puzzle will stipulate some known or assumed information about the library.
Most commonly, this will be a statement that you should assume that the cards remaining in libraries are to be assumed to be irrelevant to the puzzle.
Your Life
Occasionally, your own life total might appear to matter – for cards like Anguished Unmaking, for example. If we require you to consider your own life total in a puzzle, it will be displayed.
If your life total is not shown, you may assume it is irrelevant and effectively infinite.

When you are ready to answer, put your final winning line inside <solution> tags:

<solution>
1. First step...
2. Second step...
</solution>

Your line must be legal under the rules and must win against all possible opponent responses and blocking decisions.

Instead, Djeru's Resolve in hand has cycling {2}: I can discard it to draw the Plains, pay {2}, then play the Plains as my land for turn, giving an untapped white source.

With 5 existing lands producing 5 mana, spending 2 on cycling leaves 3, plus 1 from the new Plains gives 4 total mana available - though I'd lose access to Djeru's Resolve itself as a combat trick, which could have untapped Glory-Bound Initiate to let it attack.

Actually, since Djeru's Resolve just says "untap target creature, prevent damage this turn" without restricting it to the untap step, I could instead cast it directly on Glory-Bound Initiate to untap it and then attack with it, assuming it's not summoning sick (it appears to already be established on the battlefield, just tapped from a prior action).

This creates a choice: use Djeru's Resolve for cycling toward the Plains, or spend it to untap Glory-Bound Initiate for an extra attacker (or to save a creature from a bad trade in combat). I need to map out the full attack plan to reach 10 damage this turn, factoring in the opponent's three blockers - a 3/4 flying Shimmerscale Drake and two 2/3 Labyrinth Guardians that sacrifice themselves if targeted by a spell, which matters for how I sequence any removal or bounce effects.

Now I'm tallying my potential attackers: Kari Zev with first strike and menace (boosted to 2/4 by Hedron Blade, requiring two blockers) who also spawns a tapped-and-attacking Ragavan token, plus Pathmaker Initiate, whose unblockable-granting ability requires it to stay untapped and therefore can't attack itself if used.

But timing matters: the "attacks" trigger fires only at the moment the creature is declared an attacker, so if I cast the Aura after that step has already passed, I'd miss the trigger for the Angel token. This means to get the token, the Aura needs to be on the creature at or before declare attackers, not cast reactively during declare blockers.

So the key is timing: the trigger checks whether the ability is present when the attack event occurs, and since all attackers are declared simultaneously before triggers are checked, attaching the aura anytime before or during the declare attackers step works, but attaching after the creatures are already declared as attacking is too late. This means casting it during main phase or beginning of combat is safest, which fits well with something like Sigarda's Aid letting us flash it in.

Now I'm tallying up my available mana: two Irrigated Farmlands and three Spirebluff Canals give five mana, plus the possibility of finding an extra Plains through cycling Djeru's Resolve. I'm figuring out what spells I can fit into that mana, starting with Invocation of Saint Traft to enchant an attacker for a powerful combat trigger.

I'm also weighing Consuming Fervor for a pump, and True-Faith Censer, which is especially efficient since Sigarda's Aid lets it attach for free instead of paying the equip cost. Disperse could bounce a blocker, and Djeru's Resolve can either untap a creature or be cycled cheaply for card selection. My goal is figuring out the exact combination needed to push through lethal damage against the opponent's three blockers, keeping in mind Kari Zev's menace forces them to commit two creatures to block her.

Now I'm tallying up my available attackers for maximum damage: Kari Zev at 2/4 with first strike, the Ragavan token, Pathmaker Initiate at 2/1, and Glory-Bound Initiate at 3/1 which is currently tapped and would need to untap before it could attack or exert.

I'm also listing out potential spells to cast and their mana costs to see what combination fits.

Now I'm mapping out our mana base: two lands that tap for white or blue and three that tap for blue or red, checking how much colored mana we can actually produce toward casting everything we need this turn.

Adding up total costs: Invocation needs one generic plus white plus blue, Consuming Fervor needs red, True-Faith Censer needs two generic, and Djeru's Resolve needs white — so I'm tallying whether five lands can cover two white, one blue, one red, and two generic simultaneously.

Since Kari Zev has menace and needs two blockers, if the opponent commits both non-flying blockers there to stop her, that leaves Ragavan free to hit for 2, so I'm mapping out how the opponent would allocate blockers to minimize damage across Kari Zev, Ragavan, and the Angel.

Glory-Bound Initiate could join if untapped via Djeru's Resolve, letting me exert it for a 4/4 lifelink swing, and Consuming Fervor could pump another attacker by +3/+3 -- I'm leaning toward putting Invocation of Saint Traft on Kari Zev since she already nets an extra attacker through Ragavan.

Actually, since Invocation's Angel token trigger fires on attack declaration independent of the host creature's stats, it doesn't really matter which creature holds the aura -- the effect is the same regardless. The only question is whether the trigger still resolves and creates the Angel if the host dies mid-combat before the trigger resolves.

I'll plan the attack: Kari Zev, Pathmaker Initiate, and Glory-Bound Initiate (if untapped) all swing together, plus the Ragavan token generated from Kari Zev's attack trigger.

I'm weighing whether to use Pathmaker's ability on Kari Zev or Ragavan (both power 2) to make one unblockable, since activating it means Pathmaker can't attack. Tallying it up: Invocation (3) + Djeru's Resolve (1) + Consuming Fervor (1) equals exactly 5 mana, matching my available lands, so I'm now checking whether the color requirements (W, U, and R) all line up with what my lands can produce.

So I can cast all three spells - Invocation of Saint Traft on Kari Zev, Djeru's Resolve to untap Glory-Bound Initiate, and Consuming Fervor for a pump - using all five lands exactly, no waste. Exerting Glory-Bound Initiate gives lifelink and a power boost, and I'm weighing whether Pathmaker Initiate should also attack for maximum damage or instead use its tap ability, deciding where Consuming Fervor's +3/+3 should land, and adding up total attacking power to make sure the combined damage is lethal no matter how the opponent blocks.

With only 3 blockers available against attackers of varying power (Kari Zev 2 needing menace/double-block, Ragavan 2, Angel 4, Glory-Bound 4, Pathmaker 2), the opponent wants to use blockers efficiently on the highest-power threats rather than spending two blockers on Kari Zev's menace.

Better plan is skipping the bounce and instead using both removal spells on the Guardians while leaving Drake as the only blocker, freeing up 3 mana to cast Invocation of Saint Traft on Kari Zev — bringing total power to 10, with Drake blocking to reduce it by 4.

1180:122.1b A keyword counter on a permanent or on a card in a zone other than the battlefield causes that object to gain that keyword. The keywords that a keyword counter can be are flying, first strike, double strike, deathtouch, decayed, exalted, haste, hexproof, indestructible, lifelink, menace, reach, shadow, trample, and vigilance, as well as any variants of those keywords. See rule 613.1f.
2348:Example: A player controls one creature that “blocks if able” and another creature with no abilities. If a creature with menace attacks that player, the player must block with both creatures. Having only the first creature block violates the restriction created by menace (the attacking creature can’t be blocked except by two or more creatures). Having only the second creature block violates both the menace restriction and the first creature’s blocking requirement. Having neither creature block fulfills the restriction but not the requirement.
3803:701.60c A suspected permanent has menace and “This creature can’t block” for as long as it’s suspected.
4800:702.111. Menace
4802:702.111a Menace is an evasion ability.
4804:702.111b A creature with menace can’t be blocked except by two or more creatures. (See rule 509, “Declare Blockers Step.”)
4806:702.111c Multiple instances of menace on the same creature are redundant.
8296:Menace
8297:An evasion ability that makes creatures unblockable by a single creature. See rule 702.111, “Menace.”

That leads me to try Fervor instead, giving +3/+3 and pushing Ragavan to 5/4, plenty big enough as a decoy. So I'm reworking the plan: put Fervor on Ragavan rather than Kari Zev, leave Kari Zev at base 2 power with menace, and cut Djeru's Resolve/GloryBound out entirely to save mana — that leaves the mana curve at Invocation (3) plus Fervor (1) equaling 4, with 1 mana still spare.

Working out attackers as Kari Zev (2, menace), Ragavan (5), Angel (4, flying), Pathmaker (2), with GloryBound held back untapped and saving that mana — total power is 13. Now I'm checking how the opponent's three blockers (Drake, G1, G2) could optimally divide up against this attack, noting that Kari Zev's menace means a single leftover blocker can't stop it alone.

Testing one blocking arrangement: G2 blocks Pathmaker, leaving Kari Zev's 2 through unblocked, so only 2 damage gets through — bad for me. Then trying another split where G1 and G2 double-block Kari Zev and Drake takes Ragavan, leaving Angel and Pathmaker's 6 damage through, which is much better for me. I'm continuing to check a third arrangement where Drake blocks Ragavan and G1 takes something else.

Checking that variation: Kari Zev's 2 plus Angel's 4 get through since Drake is tied up with Ragavan, giving 6 unblocked — worse than the double-block option. The opponent will always choose whichever blocking assignment minimizes my damage, so comparing 2 vs 6 vs 6, they'd pick the first option and I'd only get 2 through — much worse than if the pump had gone on Glorybound or Kari Zev instead. This confirms that pumping Ragavan, which has no evasion, just makes it easy for a single blocker to fully neutralize, unlike Glorybound's evasion advantage.

Trying another angle: what if I pump GloryBound bigger while also keeping Kari Zev's pump? But that reintroduces the same single-block problem. Better to keep GloryBound at a modest exerted size (4) as just enough of a decoy, while putting all pump mana into Kari Zev since it's evasive. This confirms our original combo, with 7 as the practical best I can find.

Let me try something different: maybe there's a cheaper way to bounce Drake that I'm overlooking, though no cost reduction seems available for Disperse. Or maybe Drake removal isn't necessary at all — perhaps the real insight is making both Kari Zev and another creature unblockable through Pathmaker's ability combined with Djeru's Resolve's untap effect, using Pathmaker's tap ability twice in sequence.

Activating Pathmaker's ability once, then untapping it with Djeru's Resolve, would let me activate it a second time on a different creature, making two attackers unblockable in the same turn. I'm working out the sequencing — activate targeting Kari Zev first, then figure out the second target.

Since Ragavan only gets created after Kari Zev attacks, I'd need to either target Pathmaker itself before combat or wait until the trigger resolves and use the second activation on Ragavan then, assuming Pathmaker stays untapped into combat.

So one activation-tap-untap-activate sequence with Djeru's Resolve could make two creatures unblockable at the cost of Pathmaker's attack, targeting Kari Zev first for unblockable status, then untapping and potentially targeting Pathmaker itself as the second qualifying creature since Ragavan doesn't exist yet at that point in combat.

But Pathmaker can also be declared as an attacker itself since it's untapped, though attacking would tap it again anyway, using its ability then becomes irrelevant since it's already committed to combat and tapped from attacking.

Actually the key issue is timing: to make Ragavan unblockable too, I'd need Pathmaker untapped again after Kari Zev's trigger creates Ragavan, meaning a second untap effect targeting Pathmaker after its first activation - but I only have one Djeru's Resolve, so I can't untap it twice in the same turn to activate its ability against both Kari Zev and Ragavan.

That leaves 4 more mana for other spells. Both Kari Zev and Ragavan are now guaranteed unblockable, so I'm figuring out how to spend the remaining mana on Fervor and Invocation to maximize their power.

Totaling it up: Kari Zev hits for 5, Ragavan for 2, both unblockable — that's 7 guaranteed damage. The Angel from Invocation adds 4 more but isn't safely unblockable since Drake could block it, and Pathmaker can't attack since it's tapped from using its ability twice, so I'm working out the final attacker list.

Angel blocked again gives 7 total, same result. Let me try skipping the Invocation entirely and instead pumping Kari Zev and Ragavan directly with the remaining mana — splitting Fervor and Censer between them to see if that beats 7.

Actually, putting both Fervor and Censer on Kari Zev (a human, so Censer gives +2/+1) makes her 7, plus Ragavan unpumped at 2, totals 9 guaranteed damage — better than before. That uses Fervor, Censer, and Djeru's Resolve, leaving 1 spare mana that isn't quite enough for anything else useful.

Actually, putting Censer on Ragavan instead gives only 3+5=8 total, worse than stacking both pumps on Kari Zev: since Censer's human bonus makes Kari Zev the better target, both auras there give Kari Zev=7 and Ragavan=2 unpumped, total=9, confirming stacking both on Kari Zev is optimal.

Still one damage short of 10 with 4 mana spent and 1 left. Pathmaker is tapped from using its ability twice and can't attack, and Glory-Bound Initiate is also tapped with no more untap sources available, so I'm checking if there's any other angle to squeeze out that last point.

Let me try a different sequencing: instead of double-activating Pathmaker's ability on both Kari Zev and Ragavan, what if I only activate it once on Kari Zev, then use the untap effect on Pathmaker itself so it can attack normally for 2 power, leaving Ragavan blockable? Comparing the two lines - double-activation nets both Kari Zev and Ragavan unblockable but Pathmaker doesn't attack, versus this alternative where Kari Zev hits for 7 unblockable, Ragavan for 2 (blockable), and Pathmaker also attacks for 2 (blockable), still using the same 4 mana with 1 spare - now I need to check what blockers the opponent actually has available.

With three blockers alive (Drake and two others), they can easily assign two to stop Ragavan and Pathmaker while Kari Zev connects unblocked for 7, giving a total of 7 damage - worse than the double-activation line's 9. So the double-activation option, even though it sacrifices Pathmaker's attack, wins out by guaranteeing Ragavan's unblockable status too. Now I want to check a third option: single-activating on Kari Zev but leaving Pathmaker tapped entirely, saving the untap mana for something else.

Option1, using Pathmaker twice to make both Kari Zev and Ragavan unblockable, gives 9 damage—our best line so far. I just need 1 more point, so I'm checking if there's any extra value being left unused.

I still have 1 spare mana. I'm reconsidering whether Censer on Ragavan instead of the token creature would help, but vigilance doesn't matter since both are already unblocked with no combat back. Then I try a cheaper combo: putting only Fervor's pump on Kari Zev instead of splitting it, which raises Kari Zev to 5 and leaves Ragavan at 2 unpumped, totaling 7, but frees up 3 mana—enough to fit in Invocation as well.

With that mana, I add Invocation to create an Angel token with flying, needing to place it on something already attacking, so I put it on Kari Zev. The Angel is blockable by the Drake though. Recalculating: Kari Zev at 5 and Ragavan at 2 are both guaranteed unblockable via Pathmaker's double-activation, while the Angel at 4 flying can be blocked. Mana adds up exactly to 5 across Djeru's Resolve, Fervor, and Invocation. The opponent's Drake blocks the Angel since it's the only blockable creature, negating that 4 damage, while their other two blockers stay idle with nothing to block. Total damage lands from Kari Zev and Ragavan combined.

Comparing this to the Fervor plus Censer combo which nets 9 damage total, adding Invocation only nets 7 since the Angel gets blocked and wastes the mana investment, whereas Censer's guaranteed pump on the already-unblockable Kari Zev is pure value. So Fervor plus Censer remains the better line at 9 damage versus 7. Since 9 is so close to the 10 damage needed, I'm checking if there's any way to squeeze out one more guaranteed point using leftover mana, but Disperse costs too much and Invocation costs 3, leaving me stuck without a clean 1-mana source of extra damage.

Now I'm considering an alternative allocation: skip Censer entirely, keep Djeru's Resolve and Fervor for 7 total damage, freeing up 3 mana to try something else instead — but Invocation only adds a blockable Angel worth nothing extra, so that's worse. Disperse with 1 mana left over could bounce Drake, though since Kari Zev and Ragavan are already unblockable regardless of Drake, I'm not sure that bounce actually helps.

I check whether Disperse and Invocation could combine to guarantee the Angel gets through too, but the mana cost together with Djeru's Resolve exceeds what we have by a full point, so that combo doesn't fit either.

That works out to exactly 5 mana: Invocation plus Disperse. Kari Zev is guaranteed unblockable for 2, Angel is guaranteed for 4 since the Drake got bounced, but Ragavan for 2 is still blockable and Glorybound stays tapped. Opponent blocks Ragavan since it's the only legal target, so total damage lands at 6.

Actually, checking the pump split more carefully, whether Fervor and Censer both go on Kari Zev or on Ragavan instead, the combined total stays 9 as long as both stay unblockable, since it's just base power plus pump regardless of allocation - so the 9-damage line is still better than 6.

That's confirmed at 9, but I need one more point of damage. I'm second-guessing whether Pathmaker's tap ability truly requires the extra untap step, and whether there's some way to squeeze more value out of the sequencing, but the activation cost is fixed at tap, so that avenue seems closed.

The double-activation trick only nets 9, so close to 10 but not quite there. Let me check whether Glory-Bound could somehow factor in without needing untap—no, it's tapped and would need its own untap, and we only have one Djeru's Resolve which I've already committed to the Pathmaker double-tap. So instead, what if I redirect that Djeru's Resolve to untap Glory-Bound itself, letting it attack rather than using it on Pathmaker?

Running the numbers on that alternative: Pathmaker's ability used once (free) on Kari Zev to make her unblockable, Djeru's Resolve spent to untap Glory-Bound, then Fervor and Censer pumping Kari Zev, spending 4 of my 5 mana. Kari Zev comes out to 7 power guaranteed unblocked, Glory-Bound contributes 4 power but is blockable after exerting to attack, and Ragavan adds 2 more if it connects.

But Ragavan is no longer guaranteed unblockable since I didn't double-activate Pathmaker, so with three blockers available the opponent can fully block both Ragavan and Glory-Bound, leaving only Kari Zev's 7 unblocked damage — worse than the 9-damage line. So the double-Pathmaker combo protecting both Kari Zev and Ragavan is still the better play, and I'm checking whether that single spare mana in the 9-damage line could be used to also protect Glory-Bound somehow.

Trying an alternative: dropping Censer entirely and instead just using Fervor plus Djeru's Resolve for the double-Pathmaker tap costs only 2 mana, leaving 3 spare — Kari Zev hits for 5 guaranteed and Ragavan for 2 guaranteed, totaling 7, but now I have 3 leftover mana to consider spending on something else to boost the total further.

Testing if putting Censer on Ragavan instead, with Fervor on Kari Zev, changes anything - that gives 5+3=8, worse since Censer's human bonus is lost. So Censer belongs on Kari Zev, confirming the 9-total combo is optimal there.

Toughness doesn't matter here, only power for damage, and Hedron Blade's +1/+1 is already folded into Kari Zev's base. I'm also checking whether Pathmaker Initiate could somehow be reactivated a third time, but with only one Djeru's Resolve available, there's no way to untap it again.

Since we're stuck at 9 damage, I'm wondering if redirecting Djeru's Resolve to untap Glory-Bound Initiate instead of Pathmaker could close the gap, though the "prevent damage" clause on Djeru's Resolve seems irrelevant here since nothing's attacking or blocking it.

Actually, using Pathmaker's single activation on Kari Zev for guaranteed unblockability, then freeing up Djeru's Resolve to untap GloryBound instead of doubling Pathmaker, lets me pump Kari Zev with Fervor and Censer while GloryBound and Ragavan stay as blockable threats. That reworks the mana total to about 4 mana with one activation instead of two.

But testing this line: opponent has three blockers against only two other attackers, so they easily block both Ragavan and GloryBound, leaving only Kari Zev's 7 damage through — that's worse than the 9 I found earlier. So protecting both Kari Zev and Ragavan via double-activation is still the better line, since Ragavan's guaranteed 2 beats a likely-blocked GloryBound's 4 when the opponent has blockers to spare.

Now I'm checking whether there's any way to squeeze out one more point of damage — reconsidering if Censer's activation cost could shrink or if Sigarda's Aid offers any cost reduction, but neither does anything beyond what I've already accounted for. I'm also double-checking my total mana count once more to make sure I really only have 5 available, and confirming that Djeru's Resolve is indeed the only way to untap Pathmaker for the double-activation trick, so it's essential to the line.

With 5 mana total and the best combo (Djeru's Resolve, Fervor, Censer) costing 4, I'm left with 1 spare mana that isn't enough to cast Disperse or any other pump spell, so I'm exploring whether skipping Fervor and only using Censer's +2 power frees up mana that could be better spent elsewhere.

That path still comes up short (Kari Zev at 4 power plus Ragavan at 2 leaves worse totals than my existing line), so I'm checking if Djeru's Resolve itself could somehow be reused - but it's a single-use instant with no flashback, so that's a dead end. I'm now wondering if Glory-Bound Initiate has some ability I'm overlooking that could squeeze out the extra power I need.

I confirm Ragavan is 2/1 and Kari Zev with Hedron Blade is 2/4, both as expected. I'm now considering whether reordering the Pathmaker activations, targeting Kari Zev a second time instead of Ragavan, could reveal anything new, though that seems redundant since it's already unblockable.

Since Ragavan doesn't exist before combat starts, the first activation must target Kari Zev, leaving the second for Ragavan once created - so that ordering seems fixed. I'm also checking whether Pathmaker could target itself with its own ability, but that would require it to tap itself as a cost while already being tapped from the first activation, which creates a timing conflict I need to work through.

But then it's just untapped with no special status, contributing 2 blockable power. The better line is activating the ability a second time targeting Ragavan for value, giving a total of 9 - that seems to be the best confirmed line so far. With 9 so close to the target, I'm wondering if there's some additional small damage source I'm overlooking.

Reworking the math one more time: Kari Zev with pump totals 7, plus Ragavan unpumped at 2, gives 9 - I need 10. Considering how to split the pump differently: if the +2/+0 human anthem goes on Kari Zev and the haste enabler goes elsewhere, since both creatures are guaranteed unblockable, the total should just be the sum of base powers plus total pump, except for the anthem's human-specific bonus. Recalculating with both base powers at 2 each for a sum of 4...

Best placement is putting the human anthem on Kari Zev for +2 and the flat pump anywhere for +3, giving total pump of +5 and a grand total of 9 - the max these two spells alone can achieve, still one short of 10. I'm now wondering if moving the equipment from Kari Zev to Ragavan instead might free up that extra point somehow.

But Sigarda's Aid's free-attach only triggers for equipment entering the battlefield, not for repositioning something already attached - so moving Hedron Blade would cost its normal equip cost of 2 mana, and would actually cost Kari Zev its +1/+1, not gain anything overall.

Testing the redistribution anyway: moving Hedron Blade to Ragavan gives Kari Zev 1+3(Fervor)+2(Censer)=6 and Ragavan 2+1=3, totaling 9 - identical to the original total, so it's just shuffling the same +1 between creatures for no net gain, plus wasting 2 mana we don't have. Let me check whether True-Faith Censer could go on Ragavan instead while Kari Zev keeps something else.

Since Censer gives less on Ragavan, that's still not an improvement. I'm looking for a way to stack Fervor and Censer's full value on one creature while still fitting a third pump source with our single remaining mana, but Djeru's Resolve is already spent on the Pathmaker untap trick. Considering whether Fervor could serve some other purpose like evasion, but it doesn't grant unblockable, just haste.

I'm checking whether Disperse could add value by bouncing a blocker, but since Kari Zev and Ragavan are already unblockable and nothing else is attacking, removing a blocker doesn't help — Pathmaker and GloryBound aren't available to swing since they're tapped or need an untap effect we've already used. I'm rereading Censer's text more carefully and confirming it does grant +2/+1 to a Human creature, matching my earlier calculation. Verifying Fervor also gives +3/+3, so Kari Zev's total with Hedron Blade, Fervor, and Censer comes to 7 power, and now I need to add in Ragavan's contribution.

But then I pause to reconsider whether there's an alternative sequencing that lets Glory-Bound Initiate attack without Djeru's Resolve, freeing it for Pathmaker instead—only that card can untap Pathmaker to reuse its ability, so with just one copy I can't have both effects simultaneously unless there's another way to make Ragavan unblockable.

If I clear enough blockers so the opponent has one or fewer, Kari Zev's menace makes it unblocked on its own without needing Pathmaker at all—so Pathmaker's single activation could go to Ragavan instead, guaranteeing its unblockability while Kari Zev gets through naturally.

Since Pathmaker only gets one activation without untapping, that ability has to go on Ragavan. Kari Zev needs a separate solution for menace — either reduce the opponent's blockers enough to leave insufficient bodies, or accept the risk. So the plan becomes: use Pathmaker's ability on Ragavan for guaranteed unblockable, then spend remaining mana removing both Guardians so only the Drake remains, which isn't enough to satisfy Kari Zev's menace requirement.

That totals 7, still short of 9. Trying Censer instead of Fervor with the remaining 2 mana drops Kari Zev's total, making it worse.

I'm now considering bouncing the Drake with Disperse instead of sniping it, then using cheap removal on one Guardian, checking whether that leaves few enough blockers for menace to go through.

So the split-removal approach caps around 7, still below the 9 from double-activating Pathmaker with Fervor+Censer on Kari Zev. Now I want to check if combining both ideas—double-activating Pathmaker to protect both attackers while still spending on blocker removal—could push past 9.

Working through the mana, it still lands at exactly 9 with 1 mana left over that can't be spent on anything useful, since Disperse needs 2 and Invocation needs 3. That leaves me 1 short of the required 10, which is frustrating—I need to reconsider whether I'm overlooking some other line.

I go back through Kari Zev's stats and abilities again, checking whether her keywords or another creature could somehow supply the missing point of damage, but lifelink and the other abilities I'm considering don't actually add damage. I recount Kari Zev's base power and toughness with Hedron Blade's buff applied to make sure I haven't made an arithmetic error.

Right, that activation was on Pathmaker itself to enable a second use, so Glory-Bound stays tapped and adds nothing. Since Kari Zev already has menace and is hard to block, maybe I don't need to spend Pathmaker's ability on her at all — I could use the single activation elsewhere instead.

If Pathmaker targets Ragavan during declare attackers to make him unblockable, and Kari Zev's menace plus Glory-Bound as a decoy handles blockers separately, then Djeru's Resolve mana becomes free to use for something else, potentially pushing the combined damage total past both the 7 and 9 scenarios I calculated earlier.

Since we didn't cast the Invocation this line, only Kari Zev(7,menace) and Glorybound(4) are in the blockable pool, with Ragavan's 2 guaranteed separately. With 11 total blockable power against the opponent's 3 blockers (Drake, G1, G2, none removed), I need to work through how they'd distribute blocks to minimize damage.

If they put two blockers on Kari Zev to satisfy menace and the third on Glorybound, they fully absorb both attackers, leaving only Ragavan's guaranteed 2 damage getting through—which is a much worse outcome for us than I initially assumed.

This makes clear that without something adding an extra attacker (like Angel) or protecting our creatures from being blocked at all, the opponent's three blockers exactly match up with our two blockable threats, letting them shut everything down. That's why those extra tricks matter so much—they either create more unblockable-in-theory attackers or otherwise stop the opponent from having enough blockers to cover everyone.

Given that, the double-protect on Kari Zev and Ragavan looks like the strongest baseline option, since it makes both fully safe no matter what the opponent does with their three blockers. Now I want to check if I can layer in another attacker like Glorybound or Pathmaker on top of this without disturbing that protection—since any extra attacker is essentially free upside, either getting blocked harmlessly or getting through for bonus damage.

But Pathmaker ends up tapped from being activated twice, and Glorybound needs Djeru's Resolve, which is already spent untapping Pathmaker, so there's no mana room left for another attacker under this exact plan. I'm now considering whether trimming back the Fervor and Censer combo on Kari Zev slightly could free up enough mana to untap Glorybound instead, trading a bit of pump for an extra safe attacker, and I'm running the math on using only Fervor instead of both pump spells to see if that leaves enough left over.

That totals exactly 5 mana with nothing spare. But Drake can still block Angel since it's the only blockable attacker, negating that4 damage, leaving Kari Zev's5 plus Ragavan's2 for7 total - worse than the9 from the Censer line, since this wastes the3 mana on an Angel that just gets blocked.

I try fitting Glory-Bound in as a bonus without breaking the Fervor+Censer combo, but Djeru's Resolve is already committed to untapping Pathmaker, and there's no second untap effect available for Glory-Bound - so it can't be added here. After this exhaustive check, 9 looks like the practical ceiling with the double Pathmaker protection line.

I double-check whether swapping both buffs onto Ragavan instead helps: Ragavan with Fervor+Censer only gets the flat +1/+1 since it's not human, giving 6 power, plus Kari Zev's base 2, totaling 8 - worse than 9. Splitting them the other way, Fervor on Ragavan and Censer on Kari Zev, still sums to 9, confirming the total is fixed at 9 regardless of which creature holds which buff, as long as Censer lands on the human.

Since I still need one more point, I consider whether moving Hedron Blade to Ragavan instead of Kari Zev could help, but the equip cost of 2 doesn't fit the mana I have left, and it wouldn't change the total anyway. I also wonder if Djeru's Resolve's damage-prevention clause has any relevance here, but that doesn't seem to apply to this line either.

Confirming the math: two base creatures at 2 power each give 4, Fervor adds 3, and Censer adds 2 if placed on Kari Zev - totaling exactly 9, with no obvious way to squeeze out more using Ragavan or timing tricks.

Bouncing Drake doesn't seem to unlock anything extra since neither Kari Zev nor Ragavan needed it unblocked. Let me recount the mana carefully: 5 lands total, Djeru's Resolve costs 1, Fervor costs 1, Censer costs 2 — that's 4 spent, leaving exactly 1 mana unused no matter how I slice it.

So one mana is unavoidably wasted since nothing left costs less than 2. Let me check if swapping Censer for Disperse changes anything—it doesn't, since both cost 2, so the same leftover mana problem persists regardless of which 2-cost spell I pick.

Testing this combo, Angel stays vulnerable since Drake wasn't bounced, so it gets blocked for 4 negated damage, landing at only 7 total. Adding Disperse to protect Angel would push mana over budget anyway, so this path still comes up short of the 9 total from the Censer line.

Still stuck with 1 mana unused. Let me check if there's a cheaper way to enable the double Pathmaker activation without paying Djeru's Resolve's full cost, or some other creature combination that uses mana more efficiently to hit exactly 10.

Actually, what if instead of the double-activation trick, I use Pathmaker's single ability on Kari Zev before pumping, and let Ragavan take its chances against blockers while I pour all remaining mana into Kari Zev's pump. Let me recompute the mana total for that line and see if it wastes less.

If Kari Zev alone becomes guaranteed unblockable with just one Pathmaker activation, that frees up all five mana for pumping — Fervor plus Censer gets Kari Zev to 7 power guaranteed. With two mana left, I could use Djeru's Resolve to untap Glory-Bound so it can also attack, leaving one spare mana unused.

But checking that scenario: Ragavan would attack for 2, blockable and unprotected since Pathmaker was only used once on Kari Zev. That gives three attackers total — Kari Zev (7, guaranteed), Ragavan (2, blockable), Glory-Bound (4, blockable, exerted) — but the opponent has three blockers, enough to fully cover both blockable attackers, leaving only the 7 from Kari Zev getting through. That's worse than the 9 damage from the double-activation line, confirming the double-activation trick is the better play.

Since 9 is my ceiling and I need 10, I'm re-examining whether there's a way to protect additional power somehow — maybe by having the second Pathmaker activation target Pathmaker itself instead of Ragavan, letting the 2/1 attack safely too.

Actually Pathmaker can't attack if it's already tapped from activations. But what if I reorder things: activate targeting Kari Zev first, tap Pathmaker, then untap it with Djeru's Resolve, and instead of activating again, just let Pathmaker attack normally—unblockable protection lost but it still swings for 2. That gives Kari Zev fully pumped and guaranteed through, plus Ragavan and Pathmaker both vulnerable to blocks, so I need to recompute the total damage under this line.

With three blockers covering both Ragavan and Pathmaker fully, the total drops to just Kari Zev's damage, which is worse than the 9 I found earlier—so protecting Ragavan with Pathmaker's second activation, even sacrificing Pathmaker's own attack, is still the better line. That confirms 9 remains the best result in this family, so now I want to check one more variant: pumping Kari Zev before the first activation rather than after—though I already established Kari Zev needs to be at 2 power or less both when targeted and when the ability resolves for the effect to apply.

Actually if I pump Kari Zev first, its power exceeds 2 and it becomes an illegal target for Pathmaker's ability entirely, so the sequence has to be activate first while power is still 2, then pump afterward—which is exactly what I've been doing, so that ordering is confirmed correct. Since I'm still stuck at 9, I want to check whether reordering which creature gets the first free activation changes anything, like having Pathmaker target itself or another creature first so the Djeru's Resolve untap enables a different combo, but I think I've already covered the main permutations here.

Let me try skipping Djeru's Resolve entirely by having Kari Zev rely on its own menace for evasion instead of needing Pathmaker, letting Pathmaker's single free activation protect Ragavan instead, and freeing up that saved mana for pump—though when I total up Fervor, Censer, and Invocation the mana cost runs over budget.

Trying Fervor plus Censer to pump Kari Zev to 7 power with menace, skipping Invocation, leaves two mana spare for Djeru's Resolve to untap Glory-Bound as a decoy plus one extra mana. Working through the blocking math: with Kari Zev at 7 (menace), Glory-Bound at 4 (decoy), and Ragavan safely unblockable, the opponent only has three blockers to split between the two menace/decoy threats, so their best play is committing two blockers to Kari Zev to try to kill it.

Two blockers on Kari Zev negates 7, one on Glory-Bound negates 4 — that's exactly enough to fully block both, leaving only Ragavan's 2 damage unblocked. This confirms the pattern from before: this hybrid line is bad because the opponent has just enough blockers to shut it down, so I really need either the flying Angel to add an unblockable slot or a fully doubled-up protection scheme that doesn't rely on menace-decoy tricks. Nine still looks like the safest number, though I want to double-check whether Glory-Bound Initiate or Pathmaker Initiate has a Human subtype that might matter here.

Pathmaker Initiate is a Human Wizard, so I'm wondering if putting Censer on Pathmaker instead of Kari Zev would work better, giving it vigilance plus a bonus — but I need to remember that vigilance only stops a creature from tapping when it attacks, it doesn't let a {T} activated ability skip the tap cost. So swapping Censer over wouldn't actually solve the tapping problem for activating abilities.

4102:702.21a Ward is a triggered ability. Ward [cost] means “Whenever this permanent becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls, counter that spell or ability unless that player pays [cost].”
4104:702.21b Some ward abilities include an X in their cost and state what X is equal to. This value is determined at the time the ability resolves, not locked in as the ability triggers.
9246:A triggered ability that can counter spells or abilities that target the permanent with ward. See rule 702.21, “Ward.”

1180:122.1b A keyword counter on a permanent or on a card in a zone other than the battlefield causes that object to gain that keyword. The keywords that a keyword counter can be are flying, first strike, double strike, deathtouch, decayed, exalted, haste, hexproof, indestructible, lifelink, menace, reach, shadow, trample, and vigilance, as well as any variants of those keywords. See rule 613.1f.
3873:Example: Concerted Effort is an enchantment that reads “At the beginning of each upkeep, creatures you control gain flying until end of turn if a creature you control has flying. The same is true for fear, first strike, double strike, landwalk, protection, trample, and vigilance.” As that triggered ability resolves, each landwalk and protection ability from among creatures you control is granted to each creature you control.

4094:702.20a Vigilance is a static ability that modifies the rules for the declare attackers step.
4096:702.20b Attacking doesn’t cause creatures with vigilance to tap. (See rule 508, “Declare Attackers Step.”)

content.content:
3935:702.7a First strike is a static ability that modifies the rules for the combat damage step. (See rule 510, “Combat Damage Step.”)
3937:702.7b If at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike (see rule 702.4) as the combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step, instead of proceeding to the end of combat step, the phase gets a second combat damage step. The only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are the remaining attackers and blockers that had neither first strike nor double strike as the first combat damage step began, as well as the remaining attackers and blockers that currently have double strike. After that step, the phase proceeds to the end of combat step.
3939:702.7c Giving first strike to a creature without it after combat damage has already been dealt in the first combat damage step won’t preclude that creature from assigning combat damage in the second combat damage step. Removing first strike from a creature after it has already dealt combat damage in the first combat damage step won’t allow it to also assign combat damage in the second combat damage step (unless the creature has double strike).
3941:702.7d Multiple instances of first strike on the same creature are redundant.
